title: Why no dedup?
prompt: You add two `Point` objects with the same x and y to a `HashSet`, but `size()` is 2. Why?
options: The default `equals`/`hashCode` compare object identity, so value-equal Points look different
Points can't be stored in a HashSet
explanation: Without overriding, `equals` asks 'same object?' and `hashCode` is address-based — so two separately-constructed Points never match. Override both to compare by value.

title: Recall: the override skeleton
prompt: Complete the equals/hashCode overrides for a Point.
explanation: `equals(Object o)` does an instanceof check, casts, and compares fields; `hashCode()` combines the same fields via `Objects.hash`.

title: The equals/hashCode contract
prompt: Which statement MUST hold for hash-based collections to work?
options: If two objects are equal, they must have the same hashCode
If two objects have the same hashCode, they must be equal
hashCode must be unique for every object
equals and hashCode are independent and can disagree
explanation: Equal ⇒ same hash (required). Same hash ⇏ equal (collisions are allowed and resolved by equals). Override one without the other and you violate the contract.

title: Drill: count distinct points
prompt: Return the number of DISTINCT points in `points` (each `[x, y]`). Define your own `Point` class with `equals` and `hashCode`, put them in a `HashSet`, and return its size. (A class without the overrides will wrongly count every point as distinct — the hidden tests catch that.)

solution.explanation: With value-based equals/hashCode, the HashSet collapses coordinate-equal points, so its size is the distinct count. Omit the overrides and every point hashes to a unique bucket — the hidden tests with repeats would fail.

hints: Then just add every point to a HashSet and return its size.
